title: How To Stop Wasting Time And Attention On Difficult Students difficult-students/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin argues that the common instinct to give difficult students extra time, reminders, and conferences actually worsens their behavior over time by communicating that they are different and unable to control themselves. Using a composite student named Anthony as an example, he describes how years of accumulated extra attention from well-meaning teachers can convince a student he genuinely needs it, deepening the problem. His recommended fix is to cut difficult students off from excess individualized attention and instead let the classroom rules and consequences apply to them exactly as they do to every other student. He notes the transition can be quick for a student new to the classroom but slower for one accustomed to frequent individual attention, and stresses that fair, ordinary treatment — including ordinary praise rather than excessive praise — ultimately helps difficult students feel like genuine members of the class rather than outcasts.
points: Giving difficult students disproportionate individual attention can reinforce, rather than reduce, their misbehavior over time.
Treating a difficult student exactly like every other student, with the same rules and consequences, is more effective than special handling.
The transition away from special attention may take longer for students who have grown accustomed to it over multiple years.
Ordinary, proportionate praise (not excessive praise) helps difficult students feel like genuine members of the class rather than outcasts.
quotes: There is a correlation between the amount of time spent on difficult students and a worsening of their behavior.
By giving difficult students more time and attention than others, you’re telling them that they’re different, that they can’t control themselves and thus need your constant attention.

The solution is to simply cut difficult students like Anthony off from any extra time and attention (from you). Instead, let your classroom rules speak for you. If you treat difficult students like everybody else, they’ll start behaving like everybody else.

Cutting difficult students off from the attention they’ve been receiving doesn’t mean you should ignore them. It means that, when it comes to behavior issues, they should be treated the same as anyone else who breaks a rule.

Your most difficult students will appreciate being treated the same as everyone else and, as a result, seek to be a contributing member of your classroom rather than the outcast “behavior problem” they’ve been in the past.
